title: Sirhind, 1710
hook: Banda's forces take Sirhind, and land is given to those who till it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Banda Singh Bahadur, the hermit sent back into the world. Your line was called to serve. Today, Banda reaches Punjab, and the city everyone was watching. Day two hundred eighty-three.

A farmer plows land his family has worked for generations. He plants it, brings in the harvest, and then watches a large share go to a landlord who has never touched the soil, and another share go in taxes. What's left barely feeds his children. Then a rider comes to the village with news: the land now belongs to the people who work it. For many Punjabi farmers in 1710, something like that happened. It began at a city with a painful name in Sikh memory. Today: Sirhind.
screen: `LAND A FAMILY HAS WORKED FOR GENERATIONS.` → `A LANDLORD WHO NEVER TOUCHED IT.` → `THE LAND BELONGS TO THOSE WHO WORK IT.`

segments.voice: Sirhind was a rich Mughal city on the road between Delhi and Lahore. Its governor was Wazir Khan. A few years earlier, it was in Sirhind, under his authority, that Guru Gobind Singh's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were executed. They were small boys. Sikhs everywhere knew that name. When Banda Singh Bahadur arrived in Punjab with the Guru's arrows and letters, thousands joined him, many of them poor farmers. In May 1710, at a place called Chappar Chiri, his forces met Wazir Khan's army. Wazir Khan was killed, and the Sikhs took Sirhind. Historians record that the city was sacked, and that many of its people suffered. That's part of the honest story too. Then Banda did something that made him remembered far beyond the battlefield. He set up his own rule, with a fort called Lohgarh, and struck coins in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, not in his own. And in the lands he held, he broke the power of the big landlords, the zamindars, and let the land go to those who actually tilled it. How complete that change was, and how long it lasted, historians still debate. But for farmers in Banda's lands, for a time, the soil under their feet was their own. Today, at Sirhind, a great gurdwara called Fatehgarh Sahib stands where the young sons died. Sikhs go there every December, in their thousands, to remember them. Victory at Sirhind is remembered with that grief, not instead of it.
screen: `SIRHIND — WHERE THE YOUNG SONS DIED.` · `CHAPPAR CHIRI, MAY 1710.` · `COINS IN THE GURUS' NAMES.` · `THE LAND TO THOSE WHO TILL IT.` · then, large: `LAND TO THE TILLERS.`

segments.voice: Think about what you have plenty of. Not money necessarily. Maybe time on a weekend, books you've already read, clothes you don't wear, a skill someone else is struggling with, a spare room, a patient ear. Picture the person who works hard for something you have more of than you need. Choose one thing to share, and one person to share it with, this week. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sirhind. The Mughal city where the Guru's young sons were executed, taken by Banda's forces in 1710, after which land went to those who tilled it.
Your line: land to the tillers. Today, share one thing you have plenty of with someone who works hard for it. Day two hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Each December, Sikhs gather in large numbers at Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib near Sirhind for the Shaheedi Jor Mela, remembering the martyrdom of Guru Gobind Singh's youngest sons; Banda's victory of 1710 is remembered alongside it.

fork.setup: you're Banda. you've taken Sirhind. the farmers who joined you work land owned by big landlords. what do you do?
options: keep the landlords, and collect the taxes yourself.
let the land go to those who till it.
sell the land to the highest bidder.
fork.reveal: Banda broke the zamindars' power where he ruled and let the tillers have the land, though historians debate how far it went.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Sirhind (also written Sarhind), the Mughal city between Delhi and Lahore.

trapdoor: what you thought: a battle Sikhs won.
what it means: a victory remembered with grief, after which land went to those who tilled it.
what a scholar hears: Chappar Chiri, May 1710; Wazir Khan killed; Banda's coinage and seal named the Gurus; the extent of his agrarian change is debated by historians.
